questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of books sold by a store in five months:

In which month were the fewest books sold?
questions.explanation: Reading each bar directly: January=120, February=90, March=150, April=130, May=80. The smallest value is 80, which corresponds to May.
questions.trap: Students may choose February (90) because it is the second-lowest and appears earlier in the list, overlooking May's lower value of 80.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the annual revenue (in $ millions) of four companies:

What is the total revenue of all four companies combined?
questions.explanation: Add all four values: 45 + 72 + 60 + 36 = 213. The total revenue is $213 million.
questions.trap: Students may misread one bar value (e.g., read Company D as 39 instead of 36) and arrive at 216, which is not among the options, or make an addition error and pick a nearby incorrect option.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of employees in four departments of a company:

How many more employees does Engineering have than Marketing?
questions.explanation: Engineering has 60 employees; Marketing has 25 employees. Difference = 60 - 25 = 35.
questions.trap: Students may subtract Marketing from Sales (40 - 25 = 15) by misreading the question, or compute 60 - 40 = 20 by comparing Engineering to Sales instead of Marketing.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of units sold by 5 products last quarter:

What is the average (arithmetic mean) number of units sold per product?
questions.trap: Students may add only four of the five products (e.g., skip Product E), computing 1080/4 = 270 instead of 1500/5 = 300.

questions.question:
The horizontal bar graph below shows the distances (in kilometers) traveled by five delivery drivers in a day:
Driver 1: 80 km
Driver 2: 120 km
Driver 3: 95 km
Driver 4: 110 km
Driver 5: 75 km

What is the ratio of the distance traveled by Driver 2 to the distance traveled by Driver 5?
questions.explanation: Driver 2 traveled 120 km; Driver 5 traveled 75 km. Ratio = 120:75. Divide both by 15: 8:5.
questions.trap: Students may flip the ratio and compute 75:120 = 5:8, arriving at answer choice that doesn't match, or fail to simplify and not recognize 120:75 as equivalent to 8:5.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the scores of three students on two tests:
Alice: Test 1 = 70, Test 2 = 85
Bob: Test 1 = 90, Test 2 = 75
Carol: Test 1 = 80, Test 2 = 80

Column A: Alice's average score across both tests
Column B: Bob's average score across both tests
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Alice's average = (70 + 85) / 2 = 155 / 2 = 77.5. Bob's average = (90 + 75) / 2 = 165 / 2 = 82.5. Column B (82.5) > Column A (77.5). Answer: B.
questions.trap: Students may look only at Test 2 (Alice scored 85 vs Bob's 75) and assume Alice's average is higher, choosing A. But Bob's large advantage on Test 1 (90 vs 70) outweighs Alice's advantage on Test 2 (85 vs 75).

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the production (in thousands of units) of a factory over 4 years:
2020: 80 thousand units
2021: 100 thousand units
2022: 120 thousand units
2023: 90 thousand units

In which year did production first exceed 100 thousand units?
options: E. Production never exceeded 100 thousand units
questions.explanation: Reading values: 2020=80 (below 100), 2021=100 (equals 100, not strictly greater), 2022=120 (exceeds 100 for the first time), 2023=90. The first year production exceeded 100 thousand units was 2022.
questions.trap: Students may include 2021 (100 thousand) as 'exceeding' 100, choosing B. The question asks for production that EXCEEDS (is strictly greater than) 100, so 2021 does not qualify.

labels: The bar graph below shows the production (in thousands of units) of a factory over 4 years

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of customer complaints received by a call center each day of a week:

What is the difference between the highest and lowest number of complaints received in this week?
questions.explanation: Highest = Wednesday: 55. Lowest = Tuesday: 30. Difference = 55 - 30 = 25.
questions.trap: Students may find the highest as Friday (50) instead of Wednesday (55), computing 50 - 30 = 20 instead of the correct 25.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the percentage of students who passed each subject in a class of 200 students:

How many students passed English?
questions.explanation: English pass rate = 85%. Number of students who passed = 85% × 200 = 0.85 × 200 = 170.
questions.trap: Students may compute 85% of 200 as 85 × 2 = 170 (which is correct), but some may misread the graph and use 80% instead of 85%, computing 160 instead.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the quarterly profits (in $ thousands) of a small business:

Select all quarters in which profit exceeded $25,000.
questions.trap: Students may forget Q1 (just barely over $25,000) and select only B and D, or mistakenly include Q3 by misreading the graph value.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of cars sold by a dealership over 6 months:

By what percentage did sales increase from February to April?
questions.explanation: February sales = 60. April sales = 120. Percent change = (New - Old) / Old × 100 = (120 - 60) / 60 × 100 = 60/60 × 100 = 100%.
questions.trap: Students divide by the new value (120) instead of the original (60): 60/120 × 100 = 50%, choosing A. Percent change always uses the original value as the denominator.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows exports (in $ millions) from Country X over three years:

Column A: Percent increase in exports from 2021 to 2022
Column B: Percent decrease in exports from 2022 to 2023
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Column A: Percent increase from 2021 to 2022 = (180 - 150)/150 × 100 = 30/150 × 100 = 20%. Column B: Percent decrease from 2022 to 2023 = (180 - 162)/180 × 100 = 18/180 × 100 = 10%. Column A (20%) > Column B (10%).
questions.trap: Students may compute both changes as absolute differences (30 vs 18) and note 30 > 18, arriving at the correct letter A but for the wrong reason. Or they may use the same base (150) for both calculations, computing 18/150 × 100 = 12% for Column B, which still gives A > B but is arithmetically incorrect.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of items produced by a factory each week for 5 weeks:

What is the median number of items produced per week?
questions.explanation: Arrange in ascending order: 480, 500, 600, 650, 720. The median is the middle value (3rd of 5) = 600.
questions.trap: Students may use the data in the order presented (Week 1 through 5) and pick the 3rd value, which is 480, instead of sorting and finding the true median of 600.

questions.question:
The grouped bar graph below shows the number of male and female employees hired by a company in three years:
2021: Male=120, Female=80
2022: Male=100, Female=110
2023: Male=140, Female=130

In which year did female employees first outnumber male employees hired?
options: D. Female employees never outnumbered male employees
questions.explanation: 2021: Male=120, Female=80 — Male outnumbers Female. 2022: Male=100, Female=110 — Female (110) outnumbers Male (100) for the first time. 2023: Male=140, Female=130 — Male outnumbers Female again. Answer is 2022.
questions.trap: Students reading a grouped bar chart may accidentally compare male employees in one year to female employees in a different year, or they may note that 2023 has a larger total for females (130) without comparing it to males (140), concluding 2023 is the answer.

questions.question:
The stacked bar graph below shows the number of hardcover and paperback books sold by a store in three months. Each bar shows the total books sold, with the lower segment representing hardcovers:
January: Total=200, Hardcover=80 (lower segment), Paperback=120 (upper segment)
February: Total=250, Hardcover=100 (lower segment), Paperback=150 (upper segment)
March: Total=300, Hardcover=140 (lower segment), Paperback=160 (upper segment)

In February, what percentage of books sold were hardcovers?
questions.explanation: In February, hardcovers = 100 (lower segment), total = 250. Percentage = 100/250 × 100 = 40%.
questions.trap: Students may read the upper segment's value (150) as the paperback count but then compute 150/250=60% and subtract from 100% to get 40% (which is correct). But a more common error is to read the top of the upper segment (250) as the paperback value and compute 250/250=100%, getting confused. Another trap: students compute 100/150=66.7% by dividing hardcovers by paperbacks instead of by the total.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the population (in thousands) of two cities, City P and City Q, over three years:
2020: City P=200, City Q=180
2021: City P=220, City Q=216
2022: City P=242, City Q=259

Column A: Percent growth of City P from 2020 to 2022
Column B: Percent growth of City Q from 2020 to 2022
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.trap: Students may look at the absolute increase: City P gained 42 thousand, City Q gained 79 thousand. This correctly identifies Q as larger in absolute terms, but the trap is choosing A because City P's numbers look larger in the graph (242 vs 259 are close, but the bases are different — 200 vs 180).

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the monthly expenses (in $) of a household:

What percent of total monthly expenses is spent on Food and Utilities combined? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.trap: Students may compute Food + Utilities as a percentage of the non-rent expenses only: 750/(2500-1200) = 750/1300 ≈ 57.7%, misunderstanding 'total monthly expenses.'

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of units sold by 5 salespeople in a month:

The sales target is 100 units. Select all salespeople who met or exceeded the target.
questions.explanation: Alex = 85 < 100 (did not meet). Beth = 110 ≥ 100 (met). Carlos = 95 < 100 (did not meet). Dana = 70 < 100 (did not meet). Ethan = 130 ≥ 100 (met). Correct answers: Beth and Ethan.
questions.trap: Students may include Carlos (95) assuming it is close enough to 100, or misread the bar as 100. The question asks for 'met OR exceeded' the target, so 95 does not qualify.

questions.question:
The stacked bar graph below shows the revenue (in $ millions) from domestic and international sources for a company over 3 years. The lower segment is domestic; the upper segment is the additional international revenue:
Year 1: Domestic=60, International (upper segment value)=40, Total bar height=100
Year 2: Domestic=75, International (upper segment value)=55, Total bar height=130
Year 3: Domestic=90, International (upper segment value)=70, Total bar height=160

In Year 3, what is the ratio of international revenue to domestic revenue?
questions.explanation: In Year 3: Domestic = 90 (the lower segment), International = total - domestic = 160 - 90 = 70 (the upper segment represents the additional 70, NOT the full bar height of 160). Ratio of International to Domestic = 70:90 = 7:9.
questions.trap: Students read the top of the bar (160) as the international revenue value and compute 160:90, which simplifies to 16:9, not among the options. Or students use 70 (correct international value) but invert the ratio to get 9:7, choosing C instead of A.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the test scores of a class of 30 students grouped into ranges:
40-50: 4 students
50-60: 6 students
60-70: 10 students
70-80: 7 students
80-90: 3 students

Approximately what percent of students scored below 70?
questions.explanation: Students scoring below 70 are in the ranges 40-50, 50-60, and 60-70: 4 + 6 + 10 = 20 students. Total = 30. Percentage = 20/30 × 100 ≈ 66.7% ≈ 67%.
questions.trap: Students may not include the 60-70 range, counting only 4+6=10 students and computing 10/30 ≈ 33%, choosing A. Or students may include the 70-80 range, counting 4+6+10+7=27, giving 90%.

labels: The bar graph below shows the test scores of a class of 30 students grouped into ranges

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the revenue (in $ millions) of Company Z for each of the past 5 years:

Which year showed the greatest percent decrease in revenue compared to the immediately preceding year?
questions.explanation: Only years 2020 and 2023 show a decrease. 2020: (80-72)/80 × 100 = 8/80 × 100 = 10%. 2023: (108-91.8)/108 × 100 = 16.2/108 × 100 = 15%. The greatest percent decrease is in 2023 at 15%. Answer: D.
questions.trap: Students may focus on 2020 because the absolute decrease in 2020 (8 million) seems comparable and appears earlier in the data. The critical error is comparing absolute changes (8M vs 16.2M) when the question asks for percent decrease. Students who check 2020's percent decrease (10%) but do not verify 2023's (15%) will choose A.

questions.question:
The stacked bar graph below shows the number of units produced by two machines, Machine A and Machine B, in each of four weeks. The lower segment of each bar is Machine A's output; the upper segment is Machine B's additional output:
Week 1: Machine A=200, Bar total=350 (Machine B=150)
Week 2: Machine A=180, Bar total=400 (Machine B=220)
Week 3: Machine A=240, Bar total=420 (Machine B=180)
Week 4: Machine A=160, Bar total=360 (Machine B=200)

Over the four weeks, what percentage of total production came from Machine A? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.explanation: Machine A total = 200 + 180 + 240 + 160 = 780. Overall total (sum of bar totals) = 350 + 400 + 420 + 360 = 1530. Percentage from Machine A = 780/1530 × 100 = 78/153 × 100 = 26/51 × 100 ≈ 50.98% ≈ 51%.
questions.trap: Students may compute Machine B's total by reading bar heights and subtracting: B = 150+220+180+200 = 750 (correct). Then A = 1530-750 = 780 (correct). But students who read the upper segment's TOP position as Machine B's value (350, 400, 420, 360) will compute a nonsensical ratio. Alternatively, students may add Machine A and Machine B output separately and divide Machine A by Machine B instead of by the total.

questions.question:
The grouped bar graph shows the number of customers served (in hundreds) by two branches of a bank, Branch North and Branch South, over three years:
2021: North=150, South=120
2022: North=180, South=168
2023: North=198, South=210

Column A: The average annual percent growth rate of Branch North from 2021 to 2023
Column B: The average annual percent growth rate of Branch South from 2021 to 2023
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Branch North: Year 1 to Year 2: (180-150)/150 = 30/150 = 20%. Year 2 to Year 3: (198-180)/180 = 18/180 = 10%. Average annual growth = (20+10)/2 = 15%. Branch South: Year 1 to Year 2: (168-120)/120 = 48/120 = 40%. Year 2 to Year 3: (210-168)/168 = 42/168 = 25%. Average annual growth = (40+25)/2 = 32.5%. Column B (32.5%) > Column A (15%).
questions.trap: Students may compare overall growth from 2021 to 2023: North = (198-150)/150 = 32%; South = (210-120)/120 = 75%. South is still higher. But the trap is computing overall 2-year growth instead of the average of two individual annual growth rates, which may lead to arithmetic errors for some students who miscalculate.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of students enrolled in five courses:

If 25% of students in each course are seniors, and seniors from all courses together form a study group, how many students are NOT in the study group?
questions.explanation: Total students = 48+36+60+54+42 = 240. Seniors (study group) = 25% of 240 = 0.25 × 240 = 60. Students NOT in the study group = 240 - 60 = 180.
questions.trap: Students may compute 25% of each individual course and try to add them: 12+9+15+13.5+10.5=60 (correct, but Course 4 gives 54×0.25=13.5 which is not whole — some students round here and get 59 or 61 instead of 60). Then 240-60=180. Alternatively, some students compute 75% of the total directly but use 0.25 as the non-senior fraction.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the market share (%) of five companies in an industry:

The total industry revenue in 2023 was $500 million. Company A's revenue grew by 25% from 2022 to 2023. What was Company A's revenue (in $ millions) in 2022?
questions.explanation: Company A's 2023 revenue = 40% × $500 million = $200 million. Since 2023 revenue is 125% of 2022 revenue (25% growth): 2022 revenue = 200 / 1.25 = $160 million.
questions.trap: Students subtract the growth amount from the 2023 value: 200 × 0.25 = 50, then compute 200 - 50 = 150. This is wrong — the 25% is applied to the 2022 (original) value, not the 2023 value. Correct: 200 = 1.25 × 2022 revenue, so 2022 revenue = 200/1.25 = 160.

questions.question:
The grouped bar graph below shows the profits (in $ thousands) of two product lines, X and Y, over four years:
2020: X=50, Y=40
2021: X=55, Y=52
2022: X=60, Y=65
2023: X=66, Y=71.5

Select all years in which product line Y showed a higher percent growth than product line X compared to the previous year.
questions.trap: Students may compute 2023 growth rates and find both approximately 10%, then assume 'close enough' and include 2023, choosing D (all three years). The exact calculation confirms both are exactly 10% — a tie — so 2023 does NOT satisfy 'Y showed HIGHER (strictly greater) percent growth than X.'

questions.question:
The stacked bar graph below shows the breakdown of a company's workforce into full-time and part-time employees over three years. The lower segment is full-time employees; the upper segment is part-time employees:
Year 1: Full-time=300, Part-time=100, Total=400
Year 2: Full-time=360, Part-time=90, Total=450
Year 3: Full-time=400, Part-time=120, Total=520

From Year 1 to Year 3, what was the percentage increase in the ratio of full-time to part-time employees?
questions.explanation: Step 1 — Compute the ratio for each year. Year 1: Full-time/Part-time = 300/100 = 3.0. Year 3: Full-time/Part-time = 400/120 = 10/3 ≈ 3.3333. Step 2 — Percent increase in ratio = (10/3 - 3)/3 = (1/3)/3 = 1/9 ≈ 11.1%. Answer: A (11.1%).
questions.trap: Students may compute the percent increase in full-time employees: (400-300)/300 = 33.3%, choosing C. Or they compute the percent change in total workforce: (520-400)/400 = 30%. The question asks for the percent increase in the RATIO (full-time ÷ part-time), which requires computing that ratio for Year 1 and Year 3 first, then taking the percent change between those two ratio values.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the test score distributions for two classes. Each class has 20 students:
Class 1 scores: 5 students scored 60, 8 students scored 75, 7 students scored 90
Class 2 scores: 6 students scored 65, 9 students scored 80, 5 students scored 95

Column A: The arithmetic mean score of Class 1
Column B: The arithmetic mean score of Class 2
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.trap: Students may compare the simple averages of the three score values: Class 1: (60+75+90)/3=75; Class 2: (65+80+95)/3=80. This gives the correct ordering (B > A) but for the wrong reason — it ignores the weights (number of students at each score level). A student who notices Class 1 has more students at the higher score (90) may incorrectly assume Class 1 has a higher weighted mean.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the number of items (in thousands) exported by a country in each of 5 years:

If the average export value of each item was $12 in 2019 and increased by 25% by 2022, what was the total export revenue (in $ millions) in 2022?
questions.explanation: 2022 exports = 600 thousand items = 600,000 items. 2019 average value per item = $12. The value increased by 25% by 2022: new value = $12 × 1.25 = $15 per item. 2022 total revenue = 600,000 items × $15/item = $9,000,000 = $9 million.
questions.trap: Students may use the 2019 price ($12) instead of the 2022 price ($15) and compute 600,000 × 12 = $7.2 million. Or students may apply the 25% increase to the number of items exported rather than to the price per item.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the approximate population (in millions) of four cities in 2010 and 2020:
City W: 2010=2.4, 2020=3.0
City X: 2010=1.8, 2020=2.16
City Y: 2010=3.6, 2020=4.32
City Z: 2010=1.2, 2020=1.56

Select all cities that grew at exactly 20% from 2010 to 2020.
questions.trap: Students may compute the absolute increase and try to normalize: City W increased by 0.6 and City X by 0.36. Since 0.6 > 0.36, students may assume W grew faster. But 0.6/2.4 = 25% while 0.36/1.8 = 20%. The key is to use percent change (divide by the original), not absolute change.

questions.question:
The grouped bar graph shows the revenue (in $ millions) of a company's three divisions — Alpha, Beta, and Gamma — over four years:
2020: Alpha=120, Beta=80, Gamma=100
2021: Alpha=132, Beta=96, Gamma=110
2022: Alpha=145.2, Beta=110.4, Gamma=121
2023: Alpha=159.72, Beta=121.44, Gamma=133.1

If each division's revenue grew at a constant annual percentage rate, which division has the highest compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from 2020 to 2023?
options: D. Alpha and Beta are tied
E. All three divisions have the same CAGR
questions.trap: Students may observe that Alpha and Gamma both started at different values but ended with the same CAGR calculation result (1.331 and 1.3310 are nearly identical), and conclude these two are tied — but they miss Beta's much larger ratio (1.518). Students who only look at the largest absolute revenue (Alpha: $159.72M) may choose A. The insight: CAGR depends on the ratio of final to initial, not the absolute values.

questions.question:
The stacked bar graph below shows the budget allocation (in $ thousands) for two projects, Project P and Project Q, across three departments. The lower segment is Project P's allocation; the upper segment is Project Q's additional allocation:
Department A: P=240, Q=160, Total bar=400
Department B: P=180, Q=270, Total bar=450
Department C: P=300, Q=150, Total bar=450

Project P's total budget is increased by 20% and Project Q's total budget is decreased by 10%. After these changes, what is the new combined total budget (in $ thousands) for both projects across all departments?
questions.explanation: Project P original total = 240 + 180 + 300 = 720 thousand. Project Q original total = 160 + 270 + 150 = 580 thousand. New Project P total = 720 × 1.20 = 864 thousand. New Project Q total = 580 × 0.90 = 522 thousand. New combined total = 864 + 522 = 1386 thousand.
questions.trap: Students may apply the 20% increase and 10% decrease to the TOTAL combined budget rather than to each project separately. Total original = 720+580=1300. Applying net change: some students average the 20% and -10% to get +5% and compute 1300×1.05=1365, which is wrong. Others compute 1300×1.20×0.90=1404, also wrong. The correct approach: change each project's budget independently.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the enrollment numbers for a university over five years:

The university's dean claims the average percent change per year from 2019 to 2023 was 0% (i.e., the enrollment is approximately back to the starting level). A statistician counters that the arithmetic mean of the five annual percent changes is not 0%.

Column A: The arithmetic mean of the four year-over-year percent changes from 2019 to 2023
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Year-over-year percent changes: 2019→2020: (7600-8000)/8000 = -5%. 2020→2021: (8360-7600)/7600 = 760/7600 = 10%. 2021→2022: (9196-8360)/8360 = 836/8360 = 10%. 2022→2023: (8276.4-9196)/9196 = -919.6/9196 = -10%. Arithmetic mean of the four changes = (-5 + 10 + 10 + (-10)) / 4 = 5/4 = 1.25%. Column A (1.25%) > Column B (0%). The arithmetic mean of percent changes is +1.25%, not 0%, because each percent change is calculated off a different base — they do not cancel symmetrically.
questions.trap: Students may note that the ending value (8276.4) is approximately equal to the starting value (8000) and conclude the net percent change is close to 0%, choosing C. But Column A asks for the ARITHMETIC MEAN of the four individual percent changes (-5, +10, +10, -10), which equals +1.25%, not 0%. This tests understanding that arithmetic mean of percent changes ≠ overall percent change.

labels: The bar graph below shows the enrollment numbers for a university over five years

The arithmetic mean of the four year-over-year percent changes from 2019 to 2023
Column B

questions.question:
The grouped bar graph below shows the revenue (in $ millions) and costs (in $ millions) for four business units in 2023:
Unit 1: Revenue=500, Cost=380
Unit 2: Revenue=320, Cost=260
Unit 3: Revenue=450, Cost=405
Unit 4: Revenue=280, Cost=196

The company plans to close any unit with a profit margin below 15% and expand any unit with a profit margin above 25%. (Profit margin = (Revenue - Cost)/Revenue × 100).

Select all statements that are true.
options: E. Exactly two units will neither be closed nor expanded
questions.explanation: Profit margins: Unit 1: (500-380)/500 = 120/500 = 24%. Not above 25% (expand), not below 15% (close) — NEITHER. Unit 2: (320-260)/320 = 60/320 = 18.75%. Not above 25%, not below 15% — NEITHER. Unit 3: (450-405)/450 = 45/450 = 10%. Below 15% — CLOSED. Unit 4: (280-196)/280 = 84/280 = 30%. Above 25% — EXPANDED. Check statements: A: Unit 1 margin=24% < 25%, so NOT expanded. FALSE. B: Unit 2 margin=18.75%, not below 15%, NOT closed. FALSE. C: Unit 3 margin=10% < 15%, will be closed. TRUE. D: Unit 4 margin=30% > 25%, will be expanded. TRUE. E: Units 1 and 2 are neither closed nor expanded (margins 24% and 18.75%). Exactly two units — TRUE. Correct: C, D, E.
questions.trap: For Unit 1, students may round 24% up to 25% and incorrectly include it as 'expanded' (choosing A). For Unit 2, students may confuse 18.75% as being 'close to 20%' and round incorrectly. The critical insight for statement E: students must correctly identify ALL four units' statuses before they can verify that exactly two are in the 'neither' category.

questions.question:
The bar graph shows annual revenue (₹ crore) of Company XYZ:
2018: 120 | 2019: 150 | 2020: 90 | 2021: 180 | 2022: 240

By what percentage did revenue increase from 2019 to 2022?
questions.trap: Students use the new value as base: (240−150)/240×100=37.5% (option A). Percentage change always uses the original (earlier) value as denominator.

questions.question:
Same bar graph: 2018:120 | 2019:150 | 2020:90 | 2021:180 | 2022:240 (₹ crore)

Column A: Average annual revenue 2018–2020 (inclusive)
Column B: Average annual revenue 2020–2022 (inclusive)
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.trap: Students average only the endpoints: Col A=(120+90)/2=105, Col B=(90+240)/2=165. While this gives the same conclusion here, it is wrong and fails on symmetric data.

questions.question:
Same bar graph (2018:120, 2019:150, 2020:90, 2021:180, 2022:240 ₹ crore).

By what percentage did revenue fall from 2019 to 2020? (Enter number only.)
questions.trap: Students use 2020 as the base: (150−90)/90×100=66.7%. Percentage change always uses the starting (earlier) value as the base.

questions.question: Same bar graph. If 2023 revenue grows by the same ABSOLUTE AMOUNT as the 2021→2022 growth, what would 2023 revenue be (₹ crore)?
questions.trap: Students compute percentage growth 2021→2022=(240−180)/180≈33.3%, then apply it to 2022: 240×1.333≈320 (option D). The question asks for the same absolute amount, not the same percentage.

questions.question:
Same bar graph (2018:120, 2019:150, 2020:90, 2021:180, 2022:240 ₹ crore).

In which year(s) did revenue grow by MORE than 25% vs the prior year? Select all that apply.
questions.trap: Students include 2019 because 25% seems like it qualifies, or they compute (150−120)/150=20% (wrong base) and still include 2019. The boundary case of exactly 25% is the key discriminator — the question says strictly MORE than 25%.

questions.question:
Same bar graph (2018:120, 2019:150, 2020:90, 2021:180, 2022:240 ₹ crore).

Approximately what percentage of total 5-year revenue did 2022 alone contribute?
questions.trap: Students sum only recent years (e.g. 2021+2022=420) and compute 240/420≈57%. Or they omit the 2020 dip from mental addition, underestimating the total, and arrive at ~40%.
